subject: RFI: Tenant segregation, GPU tenancy, and egress controls for Helios deployment
messages:
From: Alex Turner <alex.turner@helios-fin.com>
To: laura_bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-09-18T09:22:00-07:00
Subject: RFI: tenant/network segregation + GPU tenancy questions

Laura —

Thanks for taking this RFI. As part of Helios' procurement review we need a concise description of how Redwood isolates customer workloads across the stack. Specifically:

- Network segmentation: VPC/tenant network boundaries, egress filtering, and support for private connectivity (VPC peering / PrivateLink).
- Compute tenancy: Do you co-locate GPUs across tenants? How do you avoid cross-tenant side-channel risks (MIG, host allocation, scheduling)?
- Data-in-rest and in-flight protections and key handling (KMS/HSM options).
- Auditability: sample audit log format and retention options.

Could you point us to a diagram and a brief threat-model summary that calls out mitigations for the above? Also note any compliance artifacts we can present to our infosec (SOC 2, penetration test summaries).

Thanks — aim is to finish the security pass by 2026-09-25.

— Alex Turner
Head of Cloud Risk, Helios Financial
From: laura_bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
To: Alex Turner <alex.turner@helios-fin.com>
Cc: vivek_kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.com>, marcus_lin <marcus.lin@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-09-18T11:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: RFI: tenant/network segregation + GPU tenancy questions

Alex —

Appreciate the clear list. Attached are our current artifacts: redwood_vlan_diagram_v3.png (high-level network zones), isolation_matrix_helios.xlsx (per-layer isolation and controls), and a short threat summary in the playbook PDF. Key highlights up front:

- Network: Customers are provisioned into logical tenant VPCs within the same cloud account for Redwood Private; for Redwood Hosted we use customer-specific VPCs or private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) per contract. Egress is controlled by per-tenant NAT and egress ACLs; we provide managed firewall policies and optional customer-managed firewall appliances.
- Compute/GPU tenancy: For Dedicated and Private deployments we support both single-tenant GPU pools and partitioned multi-tenant pools using MIG (when applicable). We schedule GPUs to avoid co-residency of tenants with elevated risk profiles by default and offer strict single-tenant allocation for regulated workloads.
- Crypto: Customer keys may be managed by Redwood KMS or the customer's KMS/HSM (support for external key wrapping). All model checkpoints and persistent token caches are encrypted at rest with AES-256; in-transit uses TLS1.3 with mutual TLS for inter-service trust.
- Audit and telemetry: We export structured audit logs (CSV/JSON samples attached) with request metadata, model variant, route, and latency/cost counters. Retention is configurable: 90/365/730 days per SLA.

I've looped in Vivek and Marcus for technical specifics on GPU scheduling and network isolation patterns — they will follow up with details and a short attack-surface matrix. If Helios prefers, we can also prepare a red-team/pen-test summary and provide SOC 2 Type II artifacts under NDA.

Next steps: please confirm whether you want a single-tenant Dedicated offer vs Redwood Private (on-prem/VPC) — that choice changes our recommended isolation profile and pricing.

Regards,
Laura Bennett
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference

Laura — thanks; quick clarifying Qs from our infra team after reviewing the attached diagram:

1) In your hosted model, are tenant VPCs isolated by separate AWS accounts or by logical constructs inside a single account? We need to understand blast-radius and cross-account trust.
2) For GPUs on multi-tenant pools, do you publish the probe/measurement mitigations against microarchitectural side-channels? What scheduling guarantees do you provide (time-slice separation, MIG slices)?
3) Does your KV/prefix caching persist across tenant restarts? If so, what measures ensure cache contents never leak between tenants?

Also — procurement asked for the SOC 2 quick-answers doc or pointer. Can you deliver on both the tech answers and a SOC 2 pointer by EOD tomorrow?

— Alex
From: vivek_kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.com>
To: Alex Turner <alex.turner@helios-fin.com>, laura_bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
Cc: marcus_lin <marcus.lin@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-09-19T08:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: RFI: tenant/network segregation + GPU tenancy questions — technical deep-dive

Alex / team —

Answers inline:

1) Account isolation: For Redwood Hosted we offer two deployment patterns depending on controls required:
   - Single-account logical isolation: Lightweight onboarding where tenants are provisioned as isolated VPCs/namespaces inside a single cloud account. Network ACLs, route tables, and IAM roles strictly separate tenant resources; control plane accesses resources through scoped service principals. This pattern is common for SaaS customers.
   - Per-account segregation: For customers requiring stronger blast-radius separation (Helios-style), we can provision tenant resources in dedicated cloud accounts (or org units) with cross-account trust limited to a small set of ops roles. This is our recommended default for regulated financials for Hosted.

   The attached VLAN/zone diagram shows both patterns annotated; the per-account pattern eliminates resource-level IAM overlap and allows separate billing and SCPs.

2) GPU tenancy and side-channels:
   - Dedicated: single-tenant pools guarantee no co-residency.
   - Partitioned: we use vendor MIG where available to create hardware-enforced slices. For architectures without MIG we enforce strict time-slice fencing and a cooldown period between tenant transitions; we also scrub device memory between allocations.
   - We maintain a published mitigation checklist: disabling hyperthreading on host kernels where applicable, strict CPU isolation for host processes, KSM/hugepage controls, and mitigations for branch-target/instruction-predictor classes. We will provide a focused note on microarchitectural mitigations under NDA — the red-team/pen test cover this as well.

3) KV/prefix caching: Cache stores are always namespace-scoped and access-controlled. In multi-tenant caches we include tenant-id cryptographic namespaces and short TTLs for shared caches; for high-assurance deployments we enable per-tenant cache instances with strict ACLs. Persistent caches are encrypted at rest and purged on deprovisioning.

Additional controls called out in our threat summary:
- Egress filtering by tenant with allowlists and granular egress logging.
- Service mesh sidecars enforce mTLS and policy-based access controls between microservices.
- Kernel and driver hardening on GPU hosts; minimal host tooling to reduce attack surface.
- Optional VPC endpoint-only API exposure and customer-managed NAT for zero-public-egress configurations.

Attachments (included in this thread): audit_log_sample_202608.csv (example event schema), brief attack-surface matrix (in the playbook PDF). Happy to hop on a 30-min call with your infra/infosec team to walk the diagram and scheduling semantics — suggest Tue 2026-09-21 morning PST.

— Vivek
Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference
